label: text
text: To-day's news from Shanghai is only reassuring to the extent that it emphasises the determination of the Police and the Municipal authorities to subdue the disturbances at all costs. Within a few hours the vapourings of a few students of Communist tendencies have been responsible for the creation of an international crisis which may drift along a course diametrically opposite to that intended by the first few demonstrations.

label: text
text: Not even the best friend of China would desire a replica of the Boxer Riots and of the humiliation that these eventually brought in their wake for China. But hot-headed youth inspired by sources that know not lav and order—and in fact are "up against" it—cannot be expected to stop and think of the consequences. But at the same time they themselves must share the suffering of these consequences. They cannot expect sympathy. They cannot be raised to the status of martyrs. Law and order must prevail even in China when the lives and the interests of foreigners are menaced.

label: text
text: It matters not at this distance from the scene of conflict whether the riots originated in the killing of a Chinese workman by a Japanese during the recent-cotton strike, or whether the primary cause was a desire on the part of Chinese students to escape examinations and get promotion without them. What does matter, and matter very much, is the fact that the rioters have shown their hands by the inflammatory posters they have issued broadcast over the city denouncing Imperialism and foreigners. That is proof positive that they have only been waiting for the flimiest excuse to break out of bounds and foment what really is tantamount to an anti-foreign rebellion. That is both a stupid and a dangerous policy to pursue. It must recoil on the heads of the Chinese themselves and on the Chinese as a nation.

label: text
text: If those who have the authority and the influence do not step into the breach and assist the Municipal authorities and the Police in Shanghai in the speedy restoration of order, they will assuredly regret it. There must be no weak-kneed measures or sentiment. The riots must be quelled and the originators and participants severely punished. And if that is not done within a reasonable space of time the duty of the British and the other foreigners whose interests are menaced is obvious.

The growing amount of motor traffic is revealed by the amendment of traffic regulations published in the last number of the Government Gazette. Seldom, if ever, does one see a truck in charge of a number of screeching men. The Government has wisely initiated or encouraged a system of motor haulage in keeping with modern conditions. This is all to the good and a further aid to safety, for it is admitted that proffemoving vehicles are less a danger to traffic than the slow moving kind. The speed of 15 miles and 12 miles per hour assigned to various trucks is reasonable. What is of vast importance to the efficiency with which the road haulage is used.
The additions covering ordinary vehicles are sane. A licensed driver is not to allow his vehicle to be driven by one who is unlicensed; whilst public motor vehicles are to carry a spare wheel and a serviceable kit of tools to the satisfaction of the head of the police. There should, it appears to us, be some rule covering those roads where there is either no sidewalk for pedestrians, or one of narrow dimensions making it almost impossible for it to be used. In this class of thoroughfare the pedestrian is in extreme danger of injury. A word of caution to drivers should not be out of place.

label: paragraph_title
text: How to Control Oplum.

label: text
text: One suggestion for the control of opium emanates from America. The physician attached to the Tombs Prison, New York, who has thousands of addicts under his care, proposes that the United States should solve the opium problem by prohibiting the importation of opium altogether, growing in the U.S. all the poppies necessary for the manufacture of poppies for medicinal purposes, and keeping the manufacture under Government control. He indicates where, in America, the poppies could be grown. The suggestion is a practical one. It is that of the putting your own house in order type, and on this ground alone commends itself. It has to be remembered that the Westerner has quickly come to the use of what may be termed oriental drugs and narcotics. Rightly used and under qualified medical control the moderate use of such for medicinal purposes is in order. It is the abuse that is causing so much harm—moral and physical—in those who have become addicts. Adopt this eminently sound, simple and sane question amongst Western nations, and those who are primarily responsible for the growth of the poppy will have profitable channels closed to them. It will enable those in real earnest in Eastern countries the better to grapple with an evil which has done much to sap the moral, and physical fibre of great peoples.

label: paragraph_title
text: China's Chaos.

label: text
text: Straws show which way the wind blows. A "Times" leader also shows which way thought is trending in Europe regarding things Chinese. This great paper pleads that Britain takes the lead in devising a plan for delivering China from the incubus of Civil War. Easier said than done. Any nation that takes such a lead is bound to become unpopular and misunderstood. But that must be risked where a great gain is likely to ensue. It seems remarkable that the question of China has not, so far engaged the attention of the League of Nations. Those of China's leaders who profess a wish for the country's release from all her troubles, should have no hesitation in letting such an impartial tribunal as the League of Nations attempt to devise some plan of salvation before disruption takes place, or armed interference becomes an absolute necessity. There seems no immediate prospect of peace plans coming from those who profess and call themselves leaders. There is no one to follow the example of Sir Robert Ho Tung—not even from the safe vantage ground of Hongkong—and the situation, all over the country goes daily from bad to worse.

Even a moderate sized blood vessel may become occluded partly by the clothing of the blood and partly by the contraction and retraction of the walls of the artery. Coagulation of the blood may be accelerated by (a) cold, in the form either of a stream of ice-cold water, of lint or pads of cotton wool soaked in the water, or of pieces of ice applied to the bleeding point, (b) hot water at a temperature of 115deg.F applied as a stream or in pads on the part." — Sir James Cantlie, M.M., F.R.C.S., in the British Red Cross Society's First Aid Manual, p. 84.

label: text
text: of the young people going in droves into the country to partake of milk and cream. Carew in his Survey of Cornwall (p. 68), speaking of the church ale, says that "two young men of the parish are yersly chosen by their last foregoers to be wardens, who, dividing the task, make collection among the parishioners of whatsoever provision it pleaseth them voluntarily to bestow. This they employ in brewing, baking, and other acates (provisions) against Whitsuntide; upon which holy, days the neighbours meet at the church-house, and there merrily feed on their own victims, contributing some petty portion to the stock, which, by many smalls, growth to a meetly greatness; for there is entertained a kind of emulation between these wardens, who, by his graciousness in gathering and good husbandry in expending, can best advance the church's profit. Besides, the neighbour parishes at those times lovingly visit each one another and this way frankly spend their money together. The afternoons are consumed in such exercises as old and young folk (having leisure) do accountably wear out the time withall. When the feast is ended, the wardens yield in their account to the parishioners, and such money as exceed the disbursement is layd up in store, to defray any extraordinary charges arising in the parish or imposed on them for the good of the country or the prince's service, neither of which commonly grips so much but that somewhat still remayneth to cover the purse's bottom. This custom is falling into desuetude, if it be not already discontinued.

text: It is a wonderful pageant of stirring days and captains courageous which these pictures present, beginning with the earliest attempts of the Portuguese Spaniards, British, and Dutch in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries to secure a footing for trude on the coasts of southern China, and to penetrate beyond the barriers of the Celestial Empire's splendid isolation. After the entry upon the scene of the stately orgosies of the Honourable East India Company, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, the European figures in the pageant become conspicuously British. This was to be expected, for, from 1678 onwards, when the Company established its direct and regular trade with Canton, Amoy, and (Later) Chusan, the long and often disbearing task of opening up commercial relations between China and the rest of the world—of sowing, where others have since helped fall almost entirely upon England.

label: text
text: Reviewing the Chatter Collection: A Catalogue of Pictures Relating to China, Hongkong, and Macao, 1655-1860," with descriptive letterpress by James Orange (Thornton Butterworth. £7.7s.), Mr. J. O. P. Bland writes as follows in the "Sunday Times," (London): Of the many benefits conferred by Sir Paul Chatter on his fellow-citizens of the Crown Colony of Hongkong, assuredly none will rank higher in times to come than his gift of this collection of pictures and books descriptive of the early days of the Colony and commemorative of the events which led, and the men who contributed, to its making. This handsome volume, with its eighteen plates in colour and 243 in half-tone, constitutes a very fitting and felicitous monument, not only to the public-spirited munificence of "Sir Paul," but to the memory of the stout-hearted mariners, pro-Consuls, and merchant adventurers of England who, against heavy odds, opened up new and great highways of commerce in the Far East. It contains, moreover, much more than the customary catalogue of an art collection, for Mr. Orange has done his work as editor and commentator with a through knowledge and enjoyment of his subject and much scholarly discrimination. The arrangement of the work, in appropriate sections provided with exhaustive indices, should make it of real and permanent value to students, while the numerous quotations from contemporary authors, which accompany each section, enable the casual reader to form a very vivid and accurate impression of the events and scenes they describe.

label: text

In these pictures we see the pioneers of British commerce in the Far East, living their curious life of opulent luxury. tempered by incessant humiliations, trading profitably bit on sufferance, strictly confined within the narrow space of the factories' compounds at Canton. under the kindly but watchful authority of the "Hong merchants," and threatened continually with the active hostility of mandurins, metropolitan and provincial. During the eighteenth century their trade, and with it that of heir American rivals, steadily increased, but as it grew so did the instinctive and not unjustifiable fears of the Chinese Court and mandarinate, dimly aware of the forces that lay behind the commercial advances of the outer barbarians.

label: paragraph_title
text: EVOLUTION OF THE CLIPTERR SHIP.

label: text
text: The series of paintings and drawing by W. Alexander (droughtsman attached to Lord Macartney's Embassy, 1793), by Chinnery, A. Borgel, T. Allom, and other artists, beautifully reproduced in this volume, conveys a very clear impression of the times and scenes in which these venturesme' exciles lived, moved, and had their being, up to the end of the "period of conflict" in 1860. The story which they tell is admirably annotated by well-chosen quotations from Ellis's Journal of Lord Amherst's Embassy," Bernard's "Voyages of the Nemesis," Chatterton's "Mercunile Marine," "McLeod's 'Voyage in H.M.S. Alceste,' William Hickey's "Memoirs," and the writings of Fortune, Hunter, and other authors. One of the most interesting sections of the work is that which describes the evolution of the tea and opium clipperships, things of beauty that moved in an atmosphere of poetry and romance, now lost to our machine-driven world. Their brief history of forty years was, as Chatterton says, "the golden age of the Mercantile Marine, a period when it rose to such a standard of scamanship as was never, seen before nor will ever be witnessed again." It is very fitting that this graceful monument to their memory should find its home in a Crown Colony which largely as the result of their traffic and discoveries has grown within the memory of living men from a barren island of the Ladrones to become one of the greatest seaports of the world. It is well that it should not be left to the India Home Club of New York to possess the only representative collection of paintings relating to the lives and achievements of these moneyers and acquire builders in East India.
